claim: MLL fusion proteins directly activate the expression of MYC and HOXA9 in MLL fusion-mediated leukemia.
source: In MLL fusion-mediated leukemia, MLL fusion directly activates the expression of MYC and HOXA9.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing MLL-ENL localization at MYC and HOXA9 loci (Figure 1A) and expression analysis showing high levels of these genes in MLL fusion cells.

claim: Combined expression of MYC and HOXA9 induced leukemia in mice.
source: Combined expression of MYC and HOXA9 induced leukemia, whereas single gene transduction of either did not, indicating a synergy between MYC and HOXA9.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays showing that MYC/HOXA9 combination induced leukemia while single genes did not (Figure 4E).

claim: Single gene transduction of MYC did not induce leukemia in mice.
source: Combined expression of MYC and HOXA9 induced leukemia, whereas single gene transduction of either did not, indicating a synergy between MYC and HOXA9.
evidence: Shown by in vivo transplantation experiments where MYC alone failed to induce leukemia within 200 days (Figure 3D).

claim: Single gene transduction of HOXA9 did not induce leukemia in mice.
source: Combined expression of MYC and HOXA9 induced leukemia, whereas single gene transduction of either did not, indicating a synergy between MYC and HOXA9.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transplantation experiments where HOXA9 alone failed to induce leukemia within 200 days (Figure 3D).

claim: There is a synergy between MYC and HOXA9 in leukemogenesis.
source: Combined expression of MYC and HOXA9 induced leukemia, whereas single gene transduction of either did not, indicating a synergy between MYC and HOXA9.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neither MYC nor HOXA9 alone induced leukemia, but their combination did (Figures 3D and 4E).

claim: HOXA9 sustained expression of genes implicated in hematopoietic precursor identity when expressed in hematopoietic precursors.
source: HOXA9 sustained expression of the genes implicated in the hematopoietic precursor identity when expressed in hematopoietic precursors, but did not reactivate it once silenced.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis showing HOXA9 high signature genes associated with hematopoietic identity/functions (Figure 2A,B).

claim: HOXA9 did not reactivate gene expression once silenced.
source: HOXA9 sustained expression of the genes implicated in the hematopoietic precursor identity when expressed in hematopoietic precursors, but did not reactivate it once silenced.
evidence: Demonstrated by stepwise transduction experiments showing HOXA9 could not upregulate target genes when introduced after MYC (Figure 5C).

claim: BCL2 synergistically induced leukemia with MYC.
source: Among the HOXA9 target genes, BCL2 and SOX4 synergistically induced leukemia with MYC.
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays where MYC/BCL2 combination induced leukemia (Figure 6B).

claim: SOX4 synergistically induced leukemia with MYC.
source: Among the HOXA9 target genes, BCL2 and SOX4 synergistically induced leukemia with MYC.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays where MYC/SOX4 combination induced leukemia (Figure 6B).

claim: BCL2 suppressed apoptosis in MYC-expressing cells.
source: Not only BCL2, but also SOX4 suppressed apoptosis, indicating that multiple anti-apoptotic pathways underlie cooperative leukemogenesis by HOXA9 and MYC.
evidence: Supported by Annexin V staining showing reduced apoptosis in MYC/BCL2-ICs compared to MYC-ICs (Figure 6C,D).

claim: SOX4 suppressed apoptosis in MYC-expressing cells.
source: Not only BCL2, but also SOX4 suppressed apoptosis, indicating that multiple anti-apoptotic pathways underlie cooperative leukemogenesis by HOXA9 and MYC.
evidence: Demonstrated by Annexin V staining showing reduced apoptosis in MYC/SOX4-ICs compared to MYC-ICs (Figure 6C,D).

claim: Multiple anti-apoptotic pathways underlie cooperative leukemogenesis by HOXA9 and MYC.
source: Not only BCL2, but also SOX4 suppressed apoptosis, indicating that multiple anti-apoptotic pathways underlie cooperative leukemogenesis by HOXA9 and MYC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both BCL2 and SOX4 independently suppress apoptosis and synergize with MYC.

claim: HOXA9 is a transcriptional maintenance factor that promotes MYC-mediated leukemogenesis.
source: These results demonstrate that HOXA9 is a crucial transcriptional maintenance factor that promotes MYC-mediated leukemogenesis, potentially explaining why HOXA9 is highly expressed in many leukemias.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including gene expression maintenance, inability to reactivate silenced genes, and synergy with MYC in leukemogenesis.

claim: HOXA9 is highly expressed in many leukemias.
source: These results demonstrate that HOXA9 is a crucial transcriptional maintenance factor that promotes MYC-mediated leukemogenesis, potentially explaining why HOXA9 is highly expressed in many leukemias.
evidence: Supported by analysis of patient samples from the MILE study showing high HOXA9 expression in MLL fusion leukemias (Figure 4A,B).

claim: MLL-ENL localizes to the MYC, HOXA9, HOXA10, and MEIS1 loci in HB1119 cells.
source: We observed MLL ChIP signals on the MYC, HOXA9, HOXA10, and MEIS1 loci (Figure 1A; Okuda et al., 2017), which were further confirmed by ChIP-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR experiments showing MLL enrichment at these loci.

claim: The MLL ChIP signals at target loci can be mostly attributed to MLL-ENL rather than wild-type MLL.
source: These ChIP signals can be mostly attributed to MLL-ENL as the knockdown of wild-type MLL did not affect the MLL ChIP signals (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C; Okuda et al., 2017).
evidence: Shown by ChIP experiments in cells with wild-type MLL knockdown showing maintained MLL signals.

claim: The distribution of MLL-ENL is enriched at transcription start sites in a genome-wide manner.
source: The distribution of MLL-ENL was enriched at transcription start sites in a genome-wide manner, which is similar to that of wild-type MLL observed in non-MLL fusion cell lines including HEK293T and REH (Okuda et al., 2017; Miyamoto et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by genome-wide ChIP-seq analysis showing TSS enrichment pattern.

claim: Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 are intrinsically programmed to be silenced in normal hematopoietic differentiation.
source: These results indicate that Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 are intrinsically programmed to be silenced in normal hematopoietic differentiation but are aberrantly maintained by MLL fusion proteins.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis of bone marrow cells at various differentiation stages showing downregulation during differentiation (Figure 1B).

claim: Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 are aberrantly maintained by MLL fusion proteins.
source: These results indicate that Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 are intrinsically programmed to be silenced in normal hematopoietic differentiation but are aberrantly maintained by MLL fusion proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR showing high expression of these genes in MLL fusion-expressing cells compared to differentiated cells (Figure 1B).

claim: MLL-ENL immortalized hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: HPCs exogenously expressing MLL-ENL or MLL-AF10 produced a large number of colonies in the third and fourth passages with high mRNA levels of Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 in colonies of the first passage, confirming their potent transforming capacities.
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays demonstrating sustained colony formation (Figure 1C).

claim: MLL-AF10 immortalized hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: HPCs exogenously expressing MLL-ENL or MLL-AF10 produced a large number of colonies in the third and fourth passages with high mRNA levels of Myc, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, and Meis1 in colonies of the first passage, confirming their potent transforming capacities.
evidence: Demonstrated by myeloid progenitor transformation assays showing sustained colony formation (Figure 1C).

claim: MYC expression is sufficient to induce proliferation of hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: Ectopic expression of MYC immortalized HPCs; therefore, MYC expression is sufficient to induce proliferation of HPCs.
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays where MYC-transduced cells formed colonies (Figure 1C).

claim: Endogenous Myc expression was severely diminished in MYC-immortalized cells.
source: Endogenous Myc expression was severely diminished in MYC-ICs, demonstrating that Myc expression is programed to be silenced and cannot be sustained by MYC itself.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis showing low endogenous Myc levels in MYC-ICs (Figure 1C).

claim: Myc expression is programmed to be silenced and cannot be sustained by MYC itself.
source: Endogenous Myc expression was severely diminished in MYC-ICs, demonstrating that Myc expression is programed to be silenced and cannot be sustained by MYC itself.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MYC-ICs have low endogenous Myc despite high exogenous MYC.

claim: HOXA9 immortalized hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: Ectopic expression of HOXA9 and HOXA10 (but not MEIS1) immortalized HPCs.
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays demonstrating colony formation by HOXA9-transduced cells (Figure 1C).

claim: HOXA10 immortalized hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: Ectopic expression of HOXA9 and HOXA10 (but not MEIS1) immortalized HPCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by myeloid progenitor transformation assays showing colony formation by HOXA10-transduced cells (Figure 1C).

claim: MEIS1 did not immortalize hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: Ectopic expression of HOXA9 and HOXA10 (but not MEIS1) immortalized HPCs.
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays where MEIS1 alone did not produce colonies (Figure 1C).

claim: Endogenous Myc expression was maintained in HOXA9-immortalized cells.
source: Endogenous Myc expression was maintained in HOXA9/A10-ICs, indicating that HOXA9/A10 can sustain Myc expression against differentiation-induced transcriptional suppression.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR showing high endogenous Myc levels in HOXA9-ICs (Figure 1C).

claim: HOXA9 can sustain Myc expression against differentiation-induced transcriptional suppression.
source: Endogenous Myc expression was maintained in HOXA9/A10-ICs, indicating that HOXA9/A10 can sustain Myc expression against differentiation-induced transcriptional suppression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9-ICs maintain high endogenous Myc expression unlike MYC-ICs.

claim: The colony size of HOXA9/A10-immortalized cells was relatively small compared with MYC- or MLL fusion-immortalized cells.
source: It should be noted that the colony size of HOXA9/A10-ICs was relatively small compared with MYC- or MLL fusion-ICs, suggesting a weaker proliferative potential.
evidence: Shown by colony size measurements in myeloid progenitor transformation assays (Figure 1C).

claim: HOXA9/A10-immortalized cells have weaker proliferative potential than MYC- or MLL fusion-immortalized cells.
source: It should be noted that the colony size of HOXA9/A10-ICs was relatively small compared with MYC- or MLL fusion-ICs, suggesting a weaker proliferative potential.
evidence: Inferred from the smaller colony size of HOXA9/A10-ICs.

claim: Knockdown of Myc completely repressed the colony-forming ability of MLL-ENL-immortalized cells.
source: Knockdown of Myc by shRNA completely repressed the colony-forming ability of MLL-ENL-ICs and HOXA9-ICs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by myeloid progenitor transformation assays with Myc shRNA showing loss of colony formation.

claim: Knockdown of Myc completely repressed the colony-forming ability of HOXA9-immortalized cells.
source: Knockdown of Myc by shRNA completely repressed the colony-forming ability of MLL-ENL-ICs and HOXA9-ICs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays with Myc shRNA demonstrating loss of colony formation.

claim: The maintenance of MYC expression is indispensable for immortalization of hematopoietic progenitor cells ex vivo.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that MLL fusion proteins and HOXA9 maintain Myc expression despite of the differentiation-induced transcriptional suppression, and the maintenance of MYC expression is indispensable for immortalization of HPCs ex vivo.
evidence: Inferred from Myc knockdown experiments showing complete loss of colony-forming ability.

claim: Genes highly expressed in HOXA9-immortalized cells but lowly expressed in MYC-immortalized cells are associated with hematopoietic identity/functions.
source: Genes highly expressed in HOXA9-ICs but lowly expressed in MYC-ICs (defined as 'HOXA9 high signature') were associated with hematopoietic identity/functions.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis and KEGG pathway analysis showing enrichment of hematopoietic-related pathways (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Genes highly expressed in MYC-immortalized cells and lowly expressed in HOXA9-immortalized cells are associated with anabolic pathways involved in nucleotide/protein production.
source: In contrast, genes highly expressed in MYC-ICs and lowly expressed in HOXA9-ICs (defined as 'MYC high signature') were associated with anabolic pathways involved in nucleotide/protein production (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Shown by RNA-seq analysis and KEGG pathway analysis demonstrating enrichment of biosynthetic pathways.

claim: Pathways involved in lipid metabolism were commonly upregulated in both HOXA9- and MYC-immortalized cells compared with non-immortalized c-kit-positive hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: Pathways involved in lipid metabolism were commonly upregulated in both HOXA9- and MYC-ICs compared with non-immortalized c-kit-positive HPCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis and pathway analysis of commonly upregulated genes.

claim: MLL-AF10-immortalized cells express both HOXA9 high and MYC high signature genes.
source: MLL-AF10-ICs, which express endogenous Hoxa9 and Myc at high levels (Figure 1C), expressed both HOXA9 high and MYC high signature genes (Figure 2A–C), indicating that MLL-AF10-ICs possess MYC-mediated highly proliferative potential and HOXA9-mediated hematopoietic identity.
evidence: Shown by RNA-seq analysis and gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: MLL-AF10-immortalized cells possess MYC-mediated highly proliferative potential and HOXA9-mediated hematopoietic identity.
source: MLL-AF10-ICs, which express endogenous Hoxa9 and Myc at high levels (Figure 1C), expressed both HOXA9 high and MYC high signature genes (Figure 2A–C), indicating that MLL-AF10-ICs possess MYC-mediated highly proliferative potential and HOXA9-mediated hematopoietic identity.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of both HOXA9 and MYC signature genes in MLL-AF10-ICs.

claim: HOXA9 maintains the identity of a hematopoietic precursor.
source: These differences between the HOXA9 high and MYC high signatures indicate that HOXA9 maintains the identity of a hematopoietic precursor, while MYC promotes proliferation by upregulating anabolic pathways.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq analysis showing HOXA9 high signature genes associated with hematopoietic identity.

claim: MYC promotes proliferation by upregulating anabolic pathways.
source: These differences between the HOXA9 high and MYC high signatures indicate that HOXA9 maintains the identity of a hematopoietic precursor, while MYC promotes proliferation by upregulating anabolic pathways.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq analysis showing MYC high signature genes associated with biosynthetic pathways.

claim: MYC-immortalized cells exhibited increased γH2AX, cleaved PARP, and cleaved caspase 3 levels.
source: MYC-ICs exhibited increased γH2AX, cleaved poly (ADP) ribose polymerase (PARP), and cleaved caspase 3 levels, indicative of a high degree of replication stress and apoptosis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis showing elevated apoptotic markers.

claim: Increased γH2AX, cleaved PARP, and cleaved caspase 3 levels are indicative of a high degree of replication stress and apoptosis.
source: MYC-ICs exhibited increased γH2AX, cleaved poly (ADP) ribose polymerase (PARP), and cleaved caspase 3 levels, indicative of a high degree of replication stress and apoptosis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about these markers.

claim: MYC-immortalized cells had more significant apoptotic fraction than HOXA9-immortalized cells.
source: FACS analysis with Annexin V also showed that MYC-ICs had more significant apoptotic fraction than that of HOXA9-ICs (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis with Annexin V staining.

claim: MLL-AF10-immortalized cells exhibited weak apoptotic tendencies similarly to HOXA9-immortalized cells.
source: MLL-AF10-ICs exhibited weak apoptotic tendencies similarly to HOXA9-ICs, although their MYC expression tended to be higher than HOXA9-ICs (Figures 1C and 3A).
evidence: Shown by western blot and FACS analysis of apoptotic markers.

claim: Most MYC-immortalized cells underwent massive apoptosis 1 day after cytokine removal.
source: Furthermore, most MYC-ICs underwent massive apoptosis 1 day after cytokine removal, whereas HOXA9-ICs and MLL-AF10-ICs showed relative resistance (Figure 3C) and exhibited successful recovery of the live cell population after cytokine reintroduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis after cytokine withdrawal.

claim: HOXA9-immortalized cells showed relative resistance to apoptosis after cytokine removal.
source: Furthermore, most MYC-ICs underwent massive apoptosis 1 day after cytokine removal, whereas HOXA9-ICs and MLL-AF10-ICs showed relative resistance (Figure 3C) and exhibited successful recovery of the live cell population after cytokine reintroduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis after cytokine withdrawal.

claim: MLL-AF10-immortalized cells showed relative resistance to apoptosis after cytokine removal.
source: Furthermore, most MYC-ICs underwent massive apoptosis 1 day after cytokine removal, whereas HOXA9-ICs and MLL-AF10-ICs showed relative resistance (Figure 3C) and exhibited successful recovery of the live cell population after cytokine reintroduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis after cytokine withdrawal.

claim: HOXA9 confers anti-apoptotic properties.
source: These results indicate that HOXA9 confers anti-apoptotic properties.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9-expressing cells show resistance to apoptosis.

claim: Transplantation of hematopoietic progenitor cells exogenously expressing MLL-AF10 into syngeneic mice induced leukemia with full penetrance.
source: Transplantation of HPCs exogenously expressing MLL-AF10 into syngeneic mice induced leukemia with full penetrance (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays showing 100% leukemia incidence.

claim: MYC could not initiate leukemia within 200 days in the experimental conditions used.
source: In contrast, neither MYC nor its homologue MYCN could initiate leukemia within 200 days under these experimental conditions, indicating that activation of the MYC high signature alone is insufficient for leukemogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Shown by in vivo transplantation experiments where MYC-transduced cells did not induce leukemia (Figure 3D).

claim: MYCN could not initiate leukemia within 200 days in the experimental conditions used.
source: In contrast, neither MYC nor its homologue MYCN could initiate leukemia within 200 days under these experimental conditions, indicating that activation of the MYC high signature alone is insufficient for leukemogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transplantation experiments where MYCN-transduced cells did not induce leukemia (Figure 3D).

claim: Activation of the MYC high signature alone is insufficient for leukemogenesis in vivo.
source: In contrast, neither MYC nor its homologue MYCN could initiate leukemia within 200 days under these experimental conditions, indicating that activation of the MYC high signature alone is insufficient for leukemogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of MYC and MYCN to induce leukemia in vivo.

claim: HOXA9 did not induce leukemia within 200 days in the experimental conditions used.
source: HOXA9 did not induce leukemia within 200 days either, suggesting that the HOXA9 high signature alone is also insufficient to induce leukemia.
evidence: Shown by in vivo transplantation experiments where HOXA9-transduced cells did not induce leukemia (Figure 3D).

claim: The HOXA9 high signature alone is insufficient to induce leukemia in vivo.
source: HOXA9 did not induce leukemia within 200 days either, suggesting that the HOXA9 high signature alone is also insufficient to induce leukemia.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of HOXA9 alone to induce leukemia in vivo.

claim: Both high MYC activity and HOXA9-mediated resistance to apoptosis are necessary for driving leukemogenesis in vivo.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both high MYC activity and HOXA9-mediated resistance to apoptosis are necessary for driving leukemogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neither MYC nor HOXA9 alone induced leukemia, but their combination did.

claim: Of 108 cases with MLL translocation in the MILE study, 38 were acute myelogenous leukemia and 70 were acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: Of 108 cases with MLL translocation, 38 were acute myelogenous leukemia [AML], and 70 were acute lymphoblastic leukemia [ALL].
evidence: Based on analysis of publicly available microarray data from the MILE study.

claim: Most MLL translocation cases (78.7%) were categorized in the HOXA9high/MEIS1high group.
source: Most of the cases (78.7%) were categorized in the HOXA9high/MEIS1high group, while some were in the HOXA9low/MEIS1high (13.0%) or HOXA9high/MEIS1low (8.3%) group (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown by analysis of gene expression data from the MILE study.

claim: MYC was expressed at high levels irrespective of HOXA9 or MEIS1 expression in MLL translocation cases.
source: MYC was expressed at high levels irrespective of HOXA9 or MEIS1 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of gene expression data from the MILE study (Figure 4A).

claim: HOXA9low/MEIS1high leukemia was predominantly found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: HOXA9low/MEIS1high leukemia was predominantly found in ALL, likely due to the MLL-AF4 cases, some of which do not express HOXA genes (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: Shown by analysis of gene expression data from the MILE study (Figure 4B).

claim: HOXA9high/MEIS1low leukemia was mainly found in acute myelogenous leukemia.
source: HOXA9high/MEIS1low leukemia was mainly found in AML (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of gene expression data from the MILE study.

claim: The MYC/HOXA9 combination exhibited high clonogenicity ex vivo.
source: The MYC/HOXA9 combination exhibited high clonogenicity ex vivo, with colony-forming capacity and colony size comparable to those of MLL-ENL- and HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays.

claim: A weak synergy between MYC and MEIS1 was observed in colony formation assays.
source: A weak synergy between MYC and MEIS1 was also observed.
evidence: Demonstrated by myeloid progenitor transformation assays showing increased colony formation with MYC/MEIS1 combination (Figure 4C).

claim: HOXA9/MEIS1-immortalized cells showed high Myc expression.
source: HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs showed high Myc expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and MYC-dependent proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that MYC is essential in HOXA9/MEIS1-mediated leukemic transformation.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: HOXA9/MEIS1-immortalized cells showed MYC-dependent proliferation.
source: HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs showed high Myc expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and MYC-dependent proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that MYC is essential in HOXA9/MEIS1-mediated leukemic transformation.
evidence: Shown by Myc knockdown experiments demonstrating reduced proliferation.

claim: MYC is essential in HOXA9/MEIS1-mediated leukemic transformation.
source: HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs showed high Myc expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and MYC-dependent proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that MYC is essential in HOXA9/MEIS1-mediated leukemic transformation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs require MYC for proliferation.

claim: Co-expression of HOXA9 and MEIS1 induced leukemia in all recipient mice.
source: In the in vivo leukemogenesis assays, MYC, HOXA9, or MEIS1 expression alone did not initiate leukemia, whereas co-expression of HOXA9 and MEIS1 did in all recipient mice as previously reported (Figure 4E; Kroon et al., 1998).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays showing 100% leukemia incidence.

claim: The combined expression of MYC/HOXA9 induced leukemia in 38% of recipient mice.
source: The combined expression of MYC/HOXA9 or MYC/MEIS1 induced leukemia in 38% and 18% of recipient mice, respectively, indicating a synergy of MYC with HOXA9 and MEIS1.
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays (Figure 4E).

claim: The combined expression of MYC/MEIS1 induced leukemia in 18% of recipient mice.
source: The combined expression of MYC/HOXA9 or MYC/MEIS1 induced leukemia in 38% and 18% of recipient mice, respectively, indicating a synergy of MYC with HOXA9 and MEIS1.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays (Figure 4E).

claim: There is a synergy of MYC with HOXA9 in leukemogenesis.
source: The combined expression of MYC/HOXA9 or MYC/MEIS1 induced leukemia in 38% and 18% of recipient mice, respectively, indicating a synergy of MYC with HOXA9 and MEIS1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MYC/HOXA9 combination induced leukemia while single genes did not.

claim: There is a synergy of MYC with MEIS1 in leukemogenesis.
source: The combined expression of MYC/HOXA9 or MYC/MEIS1 induced leukemia in 38% and 18% of recipient mice, respectively, indicating a synergy of MYC with HOXA9 and MEIS1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MYC/MEIS1 combination induced leukemia while single genes did not.

claim: Rapid onset of leukemia with full penetrance was observed in secondary transplantation for MYC/HOXA9, MYC/MEIS1, and HOXA9/MEIS1 combinations.
source: We observed rapid onset of leukemia with full penetrance in the secondary transplantation for the three combinations tested, confirming the presence of leukemia-initiating cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by secondary transplantation experiments.

claim: All MYC/HOXA9-induced leukemias were positive to myeloid marker Mac1 but negative to lymphoid markers B220 or CD3e.
source: All the MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemias were positive to a myeloid marker Mac1 but negative to lymphoid marker B220 or CD3e (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B), indicating that both MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-combinations induced myeloid leukemia.
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis of leukemia cells.

claim: All HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemias were positive to myeloid marker Mac1 but negative to lymphoid markers B220 or CD3e.
source: All the MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemias were positive to a myeloid marker Mac1 but negative to lymphoid marker B220 or CD3e (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B), indicating that both MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-combinations induced myeloid leukemia.
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis of leukemia cells.

claim: Both MYC/HOXA9 and HOXA9/MEIS1 combinations induced myeloid leukemia.
source: All the MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemias were positive to a myeloid marker Mac1 but negative to lymphoid marker B220 or CD3e (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B), indicating that both MYC/HOXA9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-combinations induced myeloid leukemia.
evidence: Inferred from the immunophenotype analysis showing myeloid markers.

claim: Genes involved in protein synthesis were enriched in MYC/HOXA9 leukemia cells compared to HOXA9/MEIS1 leukemia cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of MYC/HOXA9-LCs and HOXA9/MEIS1-LCs revealed that genes involved in protein synthesis (e.g. ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolic process) were enriched in MYC/HOXA9-LCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), while tumour necrosis factor α signaling and KRAS pathways were enriched in HOXA9/MEIS1-LCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Tumour necrosis factor α signaling and KRAS pathways were enriched in HOXA9/MEIS1 leukemia cells compared to MYC/HOXA9 leukemia cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of MYC/HOXA9-LCs and HOXA9/MEIS1-LCs revealed that genes involved in protein synthesis (e.g. ribosome biogenesis, tRNA metabolic process) were enriched in MYC/HOXA9-LCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), while tumour necrosis factor α signaling and KRAS pathways were enriched in HOXA9/MEIS1-LCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Shown by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: MYC-mediated anabolic pathways played more prominent roles in leukemogenesis by MYC/HOXA9 than by HOXA9/MEIS1.
source: These results suggested that these two combinations promoted leukemogenesis in slightly different ways, wherein MYC-mediated anabolic pathways played more prominent roles in leukemogenesis by MYC/HOXA9 than by HOXA9/MEIS1.
evidence: Inferred from gene set enrichment analysis showing greater enrichment of protein synthesis pathways in MYC/HOXA9-LCs.

claim: Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 have been implicated in leukemogenesis.
source: Some HOXA9 high signature genes, namely Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1, have been implicated in leukemogenesis (Zhang et al., 2013; Du et al., 2005; Delbridge et al., 2016; Steger et al., 2015), suggesting that they may be responsible for the synergy between HOXA9 and MYC.
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 were highly transcribed in hematopoietic progenitor cells transformed by combinations containing HOXA9.
source: Indeed, Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 were highly transcribed in HPCs transformed by the combinations containing HOXA9 (i.e. MYC/HOXA9-ICs, HOXA9/vector-ICs, and HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs) but not those lacking it (i.e. MYC/vector-ICs and MYC/MEIS1-ICs) (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of immortalized cells.

claim: Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 were not highly transcribed in hematopoietic progenitor cells transformed by combinations lacking HOXA9.
source: Indeed, Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 were highly transcribed in HPCs transformed by the combinations containing HOXA9 (i.e. MYC/HOXA9-ICs, HOXA9/vector-ICs, and HOXA9/MEIS1-ICs) but not those lacking it (i.e. MYC/vector-ICs and MYC/MEIS1-ICs) (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis of immortalized cells.

claim: Conditional loss of function experiments using HOXA9-ER confirmed critical regulation of Bcl2, Sox4, and Igf1 by HOXA9.
source: Conditional loss of function experiments using HOXA9 conjugated with estrogen receptor (HOXA9-ER) confirmed critical regulation of these genes by HOXA9 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis after HOXA9 inactivation.

claim: Stepwise transduction of MYC followed by HOXA9 failed to upregulate HOXA9 target genes.
source: However, stepwise transduction of MYC followed by HOXA9 failed to upregulate these HOXA9 target genes, indicating that HOXA9 could not reactivate its target genes once silenced (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis of stepwise transduced cells.

claim: Conditional inactivation and subsequent reactivation of HOXA9 within the same cell population confirmed that HOXA9 cannot reactivate its target genes once silenced.
source: Conditional inactivation and subsequent reactivation of HOXA9 within the same cell population confirmed that HOXA9 cannot reactivate its target genes once silenced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis after HOXA9 inactivation and reactivation.

claim: HOXA9 was highly expressed in all MLL fusion cell lines tested.
source: RNA-seq analysis of various human cell lines showed that HOXA9 was highly expressed in all the MLL fusion cell lines tested (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, highlighted in blue).
evidence: Shown by RNA-seq analysis of cell lines.

claim: BCL2 and SOX4 were expressed at different levels depending on the MLL fusion cell lines.
source: BCL2 and SOX4 were also expressed but at different levels depending on the cell lines.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Most MLL fusion-mediated leukemia patient samples with high HOXA9 expression expressed BCL2 and SOX4 at high levels.
source: In accord, most of the MLL fusion-mediated leukemia patient samples in the MILE study with high HOXA9 expression expressed BCL2 and SOX4 at high levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; Haferlach et al., 2010).
evidence: Shown by analysis of patient data from the MILE study.

claim: IGF1 was only expressed in MV4-11 cells despite comparable HOXA9 expression among MLL fusion cell lines.
source: IGF1 was only expressed in MV4-11 cells despite comparable HOXA9 expression among the MLL fusion cell lines, supporting the notion that HOXA9 expression itself cannot trigger the expression of silenced HOXA9 target genes.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: HOXA9 is a transcriptional maintenance factor that may be involved in the maintenance of chromatin structure previously activated by other transcriptional/epigenetic factors.
source: These results indicate that HOXA9 is a transcriptional maintenance factor that may be involved in the maintenance of chromatin structure previously activated by other transcriptional/epigenetic factors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9 maintains but cannot reactivate gene expression.

claim: SOX4 by itself showed weak immortalization capacity in myeloid progenitor transformation assays.
source: In myeloid progenitor transformation assays, SOX4 by itself showed weak immortalization capacity as previously reported (Zhang et al., 2013), while BCL2 did not transform HPCs (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony formation assays.

claim: BCL2 did not transform hematopoietic progenitor cells in myeloid progenitor transformation assays.
source: In myeloid progenitor transformation assays, SOX4 by itself showed weak immortalization capacity as previously reported (Zhang et al., 2013), while BCL2 did not transform HPCs (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown by colony formation assays.

claim: Co-expression of BCL2 with MYC led to a substantial increase in colony-forming capacity.
source: Co-expression of BCL2 or SOX4 with MYC led to a substantial increase in colony-forming capacity.
evidence: Demonstrated by myeloid progenitor transformation assays (Figure 6A).

claim: Co-expression of SOX4 with MYC led to a substantial increase in colony-forming capacity.
source: Co-expression of BCL2 or SOX4 with MYC led to a substantial increase in colony-forming capacity.
evidence: Shown by myeloid progenitor transformation assays (Figure 6A).

claim: The combined expression of BCL2 with MYC induced leukemia in vivo with a penetrance similar to that with the MYC/HOXA9 combination.
source: The combined expression of BCL2 with MYC induced leukemia in vivo with a penetrance similar to that with the MYC/HOXA9 combination (Figures 4E and 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in accord with previous reports (Beverly and Varmus, 2009; Luo et al., 2005).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays.

claim: SOX4 promoted MYC-mediated leukemogenesis in vivo.
source: SOX4 also promoted MYC-mediated leukemogenesis in vivo (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while neither MYC, BCL2, nor SOX4 alone induced leukemia within 200 days.
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays.

claim: All MYC/SOX4-induced leukemias were of myeloid lineage.
source: FACS analysis indicated that all of MYC/SOX4-induced leukemias were of myeloid lineage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis of leukemia cells.

claim: All MYC/BCL2-induced leukemias were of lymphoid lineage.
source: In contrast, all MYC/BCL2-induced leukemias were of lymphoid lineage, the half of which was B-cell type, and the other half was T-cell type, consistent with a previous report (Luo et al., 2005).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis of leukemia cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The combined expression of HOXA9, BCL2, or SOX4 with MYC alleviated apoptotic tendencies.
source: Furthermore, the combined expression of HOXA9, BCL2, or SOX4 with MYC alleviated apoptotic tendencies (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Annexin V staining showing reduced apoptosis.

claim: The expression of pro/anti-apoptotic genes was not drastically altered by SOX4 in MYC-expressing cells.
source: Although SOX4 is reported to modulate transcription of pro/anti-apoptotic genes (Ramezani-Rad et al., 2013), their expression was not drastically altered by SOX4 in this context (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR and western blot analysis of apoptosis-related genes.

claim: Multiple anti-apoptotic pathways mediated by BCL2 and SOX4 promote MYC-mediated leukemic transformation.
source: Taken together, the results indicate that multiple anti-apoptotic pathways mediated by BCL2 and SOX4 promote MYC-mediated leukemic transformation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both BCL2 and SOX4 independently synergize with MYC and suppress apoptosis.

claim: Bcl2 deletion delayed the onset of leukemia induced by MLL-AF10 in vivo.
source: On the other hand, Bcl2 deletion delayed the onset of leukemia induced by MLL-AF10 and the HOXA9/MEIS1 combination in vivo (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays using Bcl2-knockout cells.

claim: Bcl2 deletion delayed the onset of leukemia induced by the HOXA9/MEIS1 combination in vivo.
source: On the other hand, Bcl2 deletion delayed the onset of leukemia induced by MLL-AF10 and the HOXA9/MEIS1 combination in vivo (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays using Bcl2-knockout cells.

claim: Sox4 deletion delayed the onset of HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemia in vivo.
source: Sox4 deletion also delayed the onset of HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemia, although it did not affect MLL-AF10-induced leukemia (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays using Sox4-knockout cells.

claim: Sox4 deletion did not affect MLL-AF10-induced leukemia onset in vivo.
source: Sox4 deletion also delayed the onset of HOXA9/MEIS1-induced leukemia, although it did not affect MLL-AF10-induced leukemia (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays using Sox4-knockout cells.

claim: Endogenous BCL2 and SOX4 partially contribute to initiating leukemia in vivo.
source: These results indicate that endogenous BCL2 and SOX4 partially contribute to initiating leukemia in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the delayed but not completely blocked leukemia onset in Bcl2/Sox4 knockout experiments.

claim: Bcl2 deletion delayed the onset and reduced the incidence rate of MLL-ENL leukemia cells in vivo.
source: To test their roles in vivo, we transplanted Bcl2- or Sox4-deficient LCs into syngeneic mice, where we observed delayed onset and reduced incidence rate for both Bcl2- and Sox4-knockout LCs (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transplantation experiments with sgRNA-mediated knockout.

claim: Sox4 deletion delayed the onset and reduced the incidence rate of MLL-ENL leukemia cells in vivo.
source: To test their roles in vivo, we transplanted Bcl2- or Sox4-deficient LCs into syngeneic mice, where we observed delayed onset and reduced incidence rate for both Bcl2- and Sox4-knockout LCs (Figure 7C).
evidence: Shown by in vivo transplantation experiments with sgRNA-mediated knockout.

claim: Forced expression of sgRNA-resistant BCL2 restored leukemogenic potential of Bcl2-knockout MLL-ENL leukemia cells.
source: Forced expression of sgRNA-resistant cDNAs of BCL2 and SOX4 restored leukemogenic potential, validating the on-target effects of sgRNAs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments showing restored leukemia onset.

claim: Forced expression of sgRNA-resistant SOX4 restored leukemogenic potential of Sox4-knockout MLL-ENL leukemia cells.
source: Forced expression of sgRNA-resistant cDNAs of BCL2 and SOX4 restored leukemogenic potential, validating the on-target effects of sgRNAs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Shown by rescue experiments demonstrating restored leukemia onset.

claim: MLL fusion-mediated leukemia cells depend on the expression of multiple anti-apoptotic genes via HOXA9 to varying degrees to achieve survival advantages for disease initiation and maintenance.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that MLL fusion-mediated LCs depend on the expression of multiple anti-apoptotic genes via HOXA9 to varying degrees to achieve survival advantages for disease initiation and maintenance (Figure 7E).
evidence: Inferred from the partial effects of Bcl2 and Sox4 knockout on leukemia initiation and maintenance.

claim: HOXA9 regulates a variety of genes to maintain hematopoietic precursor identity and its associated anti-apoptotic properties.
source: In this study, we found that HOXA9 regulates a variety of genes to maintain hematopoietic precursor identity and its associated anti-apoptotic properties.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis and functional studies showing HOXA9's role in maintaining gene expression and preventing apoptosis.

claim: MLL fusion proteins exploit both HOXA9 and MYC downstream pathways in leukemic transformation.
source: In leukemic transformation, MLL fusion proteins exploit both HOXA9 and MYC downstream pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MLL fusion proteins activate both HOXA9 and MYC, and both pathways are necessary for leukemogenesis.

claim: MLL fusion proteins employ two arms to promote oncogenesis: MYC-mediated proliferation and HOXA9-mediated resistance to differentiation/apoptosis.
source: Thus, we propose that MLL fusion proteins employ two arms to promote oncogenesis: MYC-mediated proliferation and HOXA9-mediated resistance to differentiation/apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the distinct roles of MYC and HOXA9 in promoting proliferation and preventing apoptosis, respectively.

claim: MLL fusion-mediated leukemia does not require additional mutations in many cases.
source: However, it was unclear how MLL mutations fit this theory because MLL fusion-mediated leukemia does not require additional mutations in many cases (Andersson et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study.

claim: HOXA9 appears to maintain the intrinsic transcriptional programs of immature hematopoietic progenitor cells, which are programmed to be silenced during differentiation.
source: Thus, HOXA9 appears to maintain the intrinsic transcriptional programs of immature HPCs, which are programed to be silenced during differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from gene expression analysis showing HOXA9 maintains hematopoietic precursor genes.

claim: MYC upregulates genes involved with de novo nucleotide/protein synthesis.
source: On the other hand, MYC upregulates genes involved with de novo nucleotide/protein synthesis. This is in line with the known involvement of MYC in proliferation and associated anabolic processes (Ji et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis and established knowledge about MYC function.

claim: MLL fusion proteins activate both HOXA9- and MYC-dependent programs as alternative mechanisms to the combination of class I and II mutations.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that MLL fusion proteins activate both HOXA9- and MYC-dependent programs as alternative mechanisms to the combination of class I and II mutations.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MLL fusions activate both proliferative (MYC) and differentiation-blocking (HOXA9) pathways.

claim: HOXA9 alone cannot maintain MYC expression at a level sufficient to confer leukemogenic ability in vivo.
source: We speculate that HOXA9 alone cannot maintain MYC expression at a level sufficient to confer leukemogenic ability in vivo.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that HOXA9 alone did not induce leukemia despite maintaining some MYC expression.

claim: The therapeutic efficacy of BCL2 inhibitor has been reported in acute myelogenous leukemia including MLL fusion-mediated leukemia.
source: The therapeutic efficacy of BCL2 inhibitor has been reported in AML including MLL fusion-mediated leukemia (Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study.

claim: There is a correlation between the expression levels of HOX proteins and the sensitivity to BCL2 inhibitor in acute myelogenous leukemia patient samples.
source: Because there is a correlation between the expression levels of HOX proteins and the sensitivity to BCL2 inhibitor in AML patient samples, the aberrant expression of HOXA9 is the potential mechanism for BCL2-dependence of MLL leukemia (Brumatti et al., 2013; Kontro et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies.

claim: The aberrant expression of HOXA9 is the potential mechanism for BCL2-dependence of MLL leukemia.
source: Because there is a correlation between the expression levels of HOX proteins and the sensitivity to BCL2 inhibitor in AML patient samples, the aberrant expression of HOXA9 is the potential mechanism for BCL2-dependence of MLL leukemia (Brumatti et al., 2013; Kontro et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between HOX expression and BCL2 inhibitor sensitivity.

claim: Oncogenic MYC expression often leads to apoptosis, which needs to be alleviated by additional genetic events for leukemic cell survival.
source: Oncogenic MYC expression often leads to apoptosis, which needs to be alleviated by additional genetic events for leukemic cell survival (McMahon, 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study and established knowledge.

claim: BCL2 was highly expressed in MLL fusion-mediated leukemia.
source: BCL2 was highly expressed in MLL fusion-mediated leukemia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), and many human MLL fusion leukemia cell lines were sensitive to a BCL-2 inhibitor (i.e. ABT-199)(Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of cell lines and patient samples.

claim: Many human MLL fusion leukemia cell lines were sensitive to a BCL-2 inhibitor (ABT-199).
source: BCL2 was highly expressed in MLL fusion-mediated leukemia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), and many human MLL fusion leukemia cell lines were sensitive to a BCL-2 inhibitor (i.e. ABT-199)(Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study.

claim: High expression of SOX4 is correlated to poor survival in acute myelogenous leukemia patients.
source: High expression of SOX4 is correlated to poor survival in AML patients (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study.

claim: Ectopic expression of MYC and BCL2 induced lymphoid leukemia.
source: Ectopic expression of MYC and BCL2 induced lymphoid leukemia, whereas the MYC/SOX4 combination exclusively induced myeloid leukemia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that BCL2 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the lymphoid lineage than in the myeloid lineage in vivo, while SOX4 does in the myeloid lineage.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo leukemogenesis assays and immunophenotyping.

claim: The MYC/SOX4 combination exclusively induced myeloid leukemia.
source: Ectopic expression of MYC and BCL2 induced lymphoid leukemia, whereas the MYC/SOX4 combination exclusively induced myeloid leukemia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that BCL2 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the lymphoid lineage than in the myeloid lineage in vivo, while SOX4 does in the myeloid lineage.
evidence: Shown by in vivo leukemogenesis assays and immunophenotyping.

claim: BCL2 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the lymphoid lineage than in the myeloid lineage in vivo.
source: Ectopic expression of MYC and BCL2 induced lymphoid leukemia, whereas the MYC/SOX4 combination exclusively induced myeloid leukemia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that BCL2 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the lymphoid lineage than in the myeloid lineage in vivo, while SOX4 does in the myeloid lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the lineage specificity of MYC/BCL2-induced leukemia.

claim: SOX4 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the myeloid lineage than in the lymphoid lineage in vivo.
source: Ectopic expression of MYC and BCL2 induced lymphoid leukemia, whereas the MYC/SOX4 combination exclusively induced myeloid leukemia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that BCL2 confers relatively stronger survival advantages in the lymphoid lineage than in the myeloid lineage in vivo, while SOX4 does in the myeloid lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the lineage specificity of MYC/SOX4-induced leukemia.

claim: Blocking a single anti-apoptotic pathway may be insufficient to completely abrogate leukemic potential of HOXA9-expressing leukemia.
source: This indicates that MLL fusion proteins exploit multiple anti-apoptotic pathways and that blocking a single anti-apoptotic pathway may be insufficient to completely abrogate leukemic potential.
evidence: Inferred from the partial effects of single-gene knockout of Bcl2 and Sox4.

claim: Simultaneously blocking multiple anti-apoptotic pathways may be required for efficient molecularly targeted therapy of HOXA9-expressing leukemia.
source: Thus, simultaneously blocking multiple anti-apoptotic pathways may be required for efficient molecularly targeted therapy of HOXA9-expressing leukemia.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that multiple anti-apoptotic pathways contribute to leukemogenesis.

claim: HOX genes are known to be expressed in a position-specific manner, conferring a positional identity to a cell.
source: HOX genes are known to be expressed in a position-specific manner, conferring a positional identity to a cell (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study and established knowledge.

claim: HOXA9 unlikely functions as a major upstream factor determining tissue-specific gene expression by turning a silenced chromatin into transcriptionally active chromatin.
source: Our results suggest that HOXA9 unlikely functions as a major upstream factor determining tissue-specific gene expression by turning a silenced chromatin into transcriptionally active chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9 cannot reactivate silenced genes.

claim: HOX proteins likely play a supportive role in maintaining gene expression, which was activated by other transcriptional regulators.
source: Rather, HOX proteins likely play a supportive role in maintaining gene expression, which was activated by other transcriptional regulators.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9 maintains but cannot reactivate gene expression.

claim: HOXA9 colocalizes with active enhancer mark (acetylated histone H3 lysine 27).
source: Recently, it has been reported that HOXA9 may recruit enhancer apparatuses, as it colocalizes with active enhancer mark (i.e. acetylated histone H3 lysine 27) (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on citation to previous study.

claim: HOXA9 may support the maintenance of an active enhancer, but unlikely establishes it on silenced chromatin.
source: We speculate that HOXA9 may support the maintenance of an active enhancer, but unlikely establishes it on silenced chromatin.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that HOXA9 maintains but cannot reactivate gene expression.

claim: In MLL fusion-mediated leukemia, MLL fusion proteins directly activate both MYC and HOXA9, while HOXA9 maintains expression of MYC, BCL2, and SOX4.
source: In the case of MLL fusion-mediated leukemia, MLL fusion proteins directly activate both MYC and HOXA9, while HOXA9 maintains expression of MYC, BCL2, and SOX4, achieving high MYC activity and anti-apoptotic properties simultaneously (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq, gene expression analysis, and functional studies.

claim: MLL fusion-mediated leukemia cells possess highly proliferative potentials and survival advantages using HOXA9 as a critical mediator.
source: Thus, MLL fusion-mediated LCs possess highly proliferative potentials and survival advantages using HOXA9 as a critical mediator.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HOXA9 maintains both MYC expression and anti-apoptotic genes.
